title: The Fallen Roof
description: Simonides and the banquet hall, why order is the secret, and a first walk through your home
tryIt: Walk slowly from your front door to your bed naming six stopping places aloud, then shut your eyes and name them again backwards.

concepts.title: How it works: the poet who remembered the seats
concepts.contentHtml:
Nine guests sit down to dinner, you step outside for a moment, and the roof comes down. Could you say who was sitting where? According to legend, one man could, and that is where the memory palace begins.

Cicero tells the story in De Oratore, a dialogue about the ideal speaker that he wrote, or at least published, in 55 BC.1 The poet Simonides of Ceos was at a feast given by Scopas, a rich nobleman, at Crannon in Thessaly, and recited a poem in his honor that also spent a long time praising Castor and Pollux. Scopas, with what Cicero calls extraordinary meanness, paid only half the agreed fee and told the poet to ask Castor and Pollux for the rest.2 Soon a message came: two young men were waiting at the gate to see him. Simonides went out and found nobody. Behind him the hall fell in, and the bodies were so crushed that their families could not tell one from another.

Simonides could. He remembered the place in which each guest had sat, and told the families whose body was whose.3 Cicero then draws the lesson at the heart of this course: Simonides is said to have discovered that it is chiefly order that gives distinctness to memory.4 Anyone who wants a trained memory should fix on a set of places (in Latin, loci), turn each thing to be remembered into a mental image, and set the images in the places. Then the order of the places preserves the order of the things,5 and you use the places like a wax tablet and the images like the letters written on it.

That is the method of loci, the memory palace. You already own the raw material: every building you know well is a ready-made series of places.

concepts.title: Drill: a first walk through your home
concepts.contentHtml:
Before any rules, try the method raw. You need one building you know with your eyes shut, and home is ideal: you have walked its route so often that the order of its places costs you no effort at all. Cicero's recipe is all you need for now: places in a fixed order, and one image for each thing, set in its place.

  1. Stand at your front door, for real or in your mind. That is place 1.
  2. Walk your usual way in and stop at five more spots that stand out, such as a coat hook, a mirror, the kitchen table, the sink and the sofa. Say all six aloud, in order.
  3. Fix the direction. Always go the same way round and never double back, so the order cannot change.
  4. Put one item in each place as a vivid, slightly ridiculous image that touches the place: a goldfish flapping on the doormat, not just a goldfish.
  5. Walk the route again and look at each place in turn. Read off whatever you find there.
Drill Put these six things in your six places, in this order, then look away and walk the route. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. a goldfish
  2. a ladder
  3. a birthday cake
  4. a trumpet
  5. a snowman
  6. an umbrella

If one will not come back, go and stand in its place in your mind and look around. The place is still there even when the image has slipped, which tells you exactly what to fix: make that image bigger, stranger or noisier, and walk the route once more. Notice, too, that you never had to repeat the list to yourself. The walk did the work that repetition usually does.

concepts.title: Myth check: did the roof really fall?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Simonides invented the memory palace on the day a banquet hall collapsed.
Reality Nobody can know, and the ancient writers themselves hedged. Simonides was real: a Greek lyric poet who lived from about 556 to about 468 BC1 and seems to have spent time in Thessaly,2 where the story is set. But Cicero, writing about four centuries after the poet died, has his speaker thank Simonides, who "as people say" first invented an art of memory,3 and tells every detail as something that is said or reported. Later, Quintilian told a version in which the poem honored a victorious boxer, and he found great disagreement among his authorities over whom the poem honored and whether the house stood at Pharsalus or at Crannon.4 He also judged the part about Castor and Pollux purely fictitious,5 since Simonides himself never mentions it and would hardly have kept quiet about something so much to his credit.

So treat it as a founding legend: a story that teaches the method, not a news report. What the Romans really handed down is the method itself, and that you can test for yourself.

Wait, really? The legend has a sting in its tail. Simonides found no trace of the two young men at the gate, and in Quintilian's telling, what followed proved to him that the gods had shown their gratitude.6 In other words, Castor and Pollux paid their half of the fee by saving the poet's life.

title: Rules for Places
description: The Ad Herennium's rules: quiet, distinct, medium-sized places, spaced out, with every fifth one marked
tryIt: Walk your home route with this lesson's rules in mind, swap out any two places that look alike, and give your fifth place a golden hand.

concepts.title: How it works: a Roman rulebook
concepts.contentHtml:
You have a building and a route. Now meet the oldest instruction manual for using them. The Rhetorica ad Herennium is a Latin handbook on public speaking, addressed to one Gaius Herennius. Its translator, Harry Caplan, dates it to the second decade of the first century BC1 and calls it the oldest Latin textbook of rhetoric preserved entire. Nobody knows who wrote it. For centuries it passed as Cicero's, but modern editors agree that attribution is wrong.2 In the Middle Ages it was the foundational textbook for teaching rhetoric,3 and its short section on memory is the oldest surviving treatment of the subject.

The author splits memory in two. Natural memory is born with us. Artificial memory is strengthened by a kind of training and system,4 and it is built from two things: backgrounds (the places) and images. A background is a small, complete, conspicuous scene that natural memory grasps easily: a house, the space between two columns, a recess, an arch. An image is a figure or portrait of the thing you want to remember, set in a definite background.

Then comes the analogy that makes it click. Anyone who knows the alphabet can write down what is dictated and read it back; in the same way, anyone trained in the method can set what they hear in backgrounds and deliver it from memory. The backgrounds are very much like wax tablets, the images like letters, their arrangement like the script, and the delivery like reading.5 To remember many things you need many backgrounds, and they must form a series, so that the order can never trip you up.

concepts.title: Drill: ten places by the rules
concepts.contentHtml:
The handbook's rules for places are short and practical, and each one prevents a particular mistake. Use them to grow your six home places into a solid ten.

  1. Quiet, not crowded. Choose places in a deserted rather than a busy region: people passing to and fro blur the images, while solitude keeps their outlines sharp.1 In your mind, the house is empty.
  2. Make them differ. A run of look-alike places is a trap: the handbook warns that many identical spaces between columns will leave you unsure what you put in each.2
  3. Medium size. Places that are too large make images vague, and places that are too small leave no room to arrange them. An armchair beats a whole lawn or a keyhole.
  4. Medium light. Neither too bright nor too dim, so that shadows do not hide the images and glare does not make them glitter.
  5. Keep a gap. Space them moderately: about thirty feet, the handbook suggests.3
  6. Mark every fifth. Put a golden hand in the fifth place and, in the tenth, a friend whose first name is Decimus.4 Mark every fifth place after that the same way, and you will never lose count.

Walk your ten places forwards and backwards until you can name them without effort. The handbook asks you to study your places with special care so that they cling lastingly in your memory: the images will change every time you use the palace, but the places must stay fixed.

concepts.title: Myth check: does it have to be a palace?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth You need a grand building, the bigger the better, and it must be somewhere you know intimately.
Reality Bigger is worse: the handbook wants places of moderate size, because huge ones make images vague. Nor must they be real. If your stock of places runs short, it says, the imagination can embrace any region and build whatever settings you need.1 A modern experiment agrees. In 2012 Legge and colleagues had people use the method on 10 lists of 11 unrelated words;2 some built their palace from a virtual environment they had studied only briefly on a computer, while others used highly familiar places. The virtual palaces worked as well as the familiar ones, measured against people given no method.3 For beginners at least, the authors concluded, a highly detailed environment does not give substantially better memory.

Familiar places are still the usual choice, because they come free: you already know their order. The champions in the 2003 brain-imaging study you will meet in lesson 4 relied on routes that were typically real and familiar.4

Wait, really? The handbook's reason for spacing places about thirty feet apart is optical. Like the external eye, it says, the inner eye of thought is less powerful when you move the object of sight too near or too far away. Even in imagination, you need a comfortable viewing distance, so stand back from each place far enough to see the whole of it.

title: Placing and Walking
description: Loading a list into your palace, reading it back in both directions, and using the palace again
tryIt: Put tonight's shopping list into the first ten places of your palace, then recall it at the shop without looking at the list.

concepts.title: How it works: one series, two directions
concepts.contentHtml:
Someone hands you ten errands and no paper. Walk once through your palace, leaving an image in each place, and the list is stored in order. Better still, it comes back in either direction. The Ad Herennium explains why: because the places form a series, you can start from any place you like and go forwards or backwards.

Its example is a line of friends. If you saw a number of people you know standing in a certain order, it would make no difference whether you named them from the head of the line, the foot or the middle.1 Places arranged in order work the same way: reminded by the images, you can repeat what you stored, proceeding in either direction from any place you please.2 Modern researchers describe the same routine. You imagine walking through a familiar environment,3 "placing" each item in a specific location; to recall, you walk it again, "looking" for the items in order.

Does it work outside a Roman law court? In 2021 Twomey and Kroneisen pooled 13 randomized controlled trials, mostly run in universities, and found a4 medium effect in favor of the method (an effect size of 0.65). It held up when they adjusted for publication bias and removed studies one at a time. They also flagged a weakness: most trials did not report how they randomized people, so the risk of bias is high.5 Their verdict was good initial support, not the last word.

concepts.title: Drill: the shopping list
concepts.contentHtml:
Time to load the palace you built in lesson 2. A shopping list is the classic first job: ten things in no particular order that you will need in a hurry later, with no paper in sight.

  1. Arrive at place 1 and see it clearly first: the color of the door, the handle, the mat.
  2. Make the item act on the place. Eggs smashing against the front door beat a box of eggs sitting nearby. Big, moving and odd is the goal.
  3. Linger for a breath, then move on. One item per place; never crowd two into one.
  4. Check your count at the golden hand. The fifth item should be sitting on it. If it is not, you have skipped a place.
  5. Walk back from 10 to 1, reading each image, then forwards once more. Reading in both directions is your proof that the list is really stored.
Drill Place these ten items in your ten places, then read them back forwards and backwards without looking. The quiz will ask for the seventh item and for the list read backwards.
  1. eggs
  2. toothpaste
  3. bananas
  4. lightbulbs
  5. teabags
  6. wrapping paper
  7. lemons
  8. batteries
  9. cheese
  10. bin bags

If a gap appears, do not panic and do not start again from the door. Stand in the empty place and look: usually a faint image is still there. Make it louder and carry on walking. Then, at the shop, walk the palace aisle by aisle and tick things off as you meet them.

concepts.title: Myth check: a full palace is used up
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Once a palace is full it is spent: reuse it and the old list will tangle with the new one.
Reality The Ad Herennium expected reuse. Images, like letters, are effaced when we make no use of them, it says, but the backgrounds, like wax tablets, should abide.1 Modern tests broadly agree. In 2006 Massen and Vaterrodt-Plünnecke looked for proactive interference, where earlier lists get in the way of later ones, a real risk when the same places hold list after list.2 When every list came from the same category, interference did appear, but it was no worse for the method of loci than for two methods that use no fixed places, the link method and simple rehearsal.3

There is a practical catch, and trainers plan for it. In a 2017 training study, people built four routes, and their training plans said which route to use each day, partly to reduce interference from lists memorized on preceding days.4 So keep a few palaces and use them in turn, and let yesterday's images fade before you reuse a route for something similar.

Wait, really? The method can even push back against interference. In a 2014 study by Bass and Oswald, people taught the method in a single 25-minute session recalled about 70% of a list built to suffer heavy interference,5 against about 50% for people without it.6 The authors were careful to add that they could not rule out that any training session at all would have helped.

title: The Champions' Secret
description: What Maguire's 2003 brain scans found in memory champions, and a second palace outdoors
tryIt: On your next walk to the shops or a bus stop, pick ten distinct places along the way and say them in order on the way home.

concepts.title: How it works: scanning the champions
concepts.contentHtml:
At the World Memory Championships, top competitors memorize hundreds of words or digits within minutes.1 Are they a different kind of human? In a study published in 2003, Eleanor Maguire of University College London and her colleagues went looking inside their heads.

They tested ten superior memorizers: eight who were, or had been, placed at the highest levels of the World Memory Championships,2 plus two others already studied for extraordinary feats of memory. The ten were compared with ten matched volunteers. The team used three tools: standard tests of memory and reasoning, structural brain scans to look for differences in gray matter, and functional MRI while everyone learned three kinds of material: three-digit numbers, faces and snowflakes.

Superior memory was not driven by exceptional intellectual ability or by structural brain differences.3 What differed was how the brain worked during learning. The champions preferentially engaged three regions, the medial parietal cortex, the retrosplenial cortex and the right posterior hippocampus, which the authors describe as important for memory and implicated in spatial memory and navigation. In the paper's own summary, the champions used a spatial learning strategy.4 Afterwards every one of them said they had used mnemonics, and nine of the ten had used the method of loci for some or all of the tasks.5

The team was careful about what this proved. The pattern might reflect the champions' many years of practice, or a special facility for the method, and they wrote that studying people newly taught the method of loci would be an important next step.6 Lesson 5 is that study.

concepts.title: Drill: a second palace outdoors
concepts.contentHtml:
Champions do not get by with one palace, and neither will you for long. In the training study you will meet in lesson 5, novices were taught their first route inside and outside the research institute, during a two-hour introductory course.1 An outdoor route makes a good second palace: its places are naturally spread out and unlike each other, just as the rules ask.

  1. Pick a walk you know cold, such as the way to the shops, the bus stop or round the park. Always walk it in the same direction.
  2. Choose ten places along it that differ in shape: a gate, a postbox, a bench, a tree, a bus shelter. Avoid five identical lamp posts.
  3. Mark the fifth and the tenth as before, with a golden hand and with your friend Decimus.
  4. Walk it twice in your head, forwards and backwards, before you load anything.
  5. Load the drill below, one image per place, then walk the route again and read the images off.
Drill Place these ten words along your outdoor route, then walk it in your head and read them back. The quiz will ask for the fifth word and for the order of several.
  1. anchor
  2. violin
  3. cactus
  4. helmet
  5. pearl
  6. kettle
  7. rocket
  8. scarf
  9. lighthouse
  10. tortoise

Notice how the outdoor route feels different from home: more air between the places, more variety in their shapes. Neither palace is better. Having both means you can use them in turn, which, as lesson 3 showed, helps keep one list from tangling with the next.

concepts.title: Myth check: born with a special brain
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Memory champions are born with photographic memories or unusual brains, so the method is not for ordinary people.
Reality Maguire's team found neither exceptional intellect nor any structural difference in the champions' brains. On a reading test that estimates verbal IQ, the champions averaged 111 and the controls 112. What the champions did have was practice: more than eleven years of using mnemonics, on average.1 A 2017 study of 23 memory athletes from the top 50 of the world rankings2 found the same story in their own words: every one of them attributed their skills to deliberate training in mnemonic strategies.3

Wait, really? The champions' lead depended on the material. It was greatest for three-digit numbers, smaller for faces and almost nothing for snowflakes,4 which the researchers chose because they are unusual and hard to put into words. A memory palace stores images of things you can name or picture. Give a champion something that resists both, and they look much like the rest of us. That is strong evidence that the skill lives in the method, not in some special hardware, and it is a method you are already using.

title: Six Weeks of Training
description: Dresler's 2017 training study, what lasted four months, and what the method cannot promise
tryIt: Ask someone to read you twelve random words once, place them along a route, and write down as many as you can twenty minutes later.

concepts.title: How it works: from 26 words to 62
concepts.contentHtml:
Here is the experiment Maguire's team asked for. Can ordinary people taught the method of loci start to perform like memory athletes, and do their brains start to work like athletes' brains?

In 2017 Martin Dresler and colleagues published the answer in the journal Neuron. First they scanned 23 memory athletes from the top 50 of the world rankings. Seventeen of them learned 72 words in the scanner and recalled 70.8 on average 20 minutes later, against 39.9 for matched controls.1 Then came the training study. Fifty-one men, all new to mnemonics, were split between three groups: six weeks of method-of-loci training (40 sessions of 30 minutes),2 six weeks of a working-memory game called the n-back, or no training at all.

The loci group more than doubled their scores, from an average of 26 words out of 72 to 62.3 Their improvement was significantly greater than in either control group, and it persisted at a follow-up four months later.4 Their brains changed too, though not in shape: patterns of functional connectivity, how strongly regions work in step, shifted towards the athletes' patterns, and the people whose patterns shifted most improved most. In the authors' words, the training drove distributed rather than regional changes,5 reorganizing networks across the brain.

Two limits are worth keeping in mind. The trainees were all men, with an average age of 24,6 and they practiced lists of words. What held for them may not hold for everyone, or for every kind of material.

concepts.title: Drill: a training week
concepts.contentHtml:
You do not need a laboratory to train like Dresler's volunteers. Their plan was simple: a two-hour introduction and a first route, then 30 minutes a day for 40 days on a web-based training platform at home.1 In the first two weeks they built and memorized three more routes;2 for the next four weeks they memorized lists of random words or images on those four routes, with the length of each list adjusted to how well they were doing.3

  1. Build up to four routes. You have home and an outdoor walk. Add two more this week: a workplace, a school, a relative's house.
  2. Use them in turn, one route per session, so each new list lands on a route that has had time to clear.
  3. Train little and often. A short session on most days is the habit to build; the Ad Herennium told its readers to practice placing images every day.4
  4. Test like the scientists. Recall each list after about 20 minutes, and again the next day.
  5. Raise the bar when you get every word, and lower it when you miss several.
Drill Extend your home palace to twelve places (two past Decimus) and place these twelve words. Five are abstract, so turn each into something you can see. The quiz will ask for the tenth word and for the order of several.
  1. volcano
  2. freedom
  3. umbrella
  4. piano
  5. honesty
  6. penguin
  7. thunder
  8. history
  9. cushion
  10. jealousy
  11. bicycle
  12. silence

concepts.title: Myth check: a palace against forgetting?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Memory palaces exercise the brain like a muscle, so they will protect you against dementia.
Reality None of the studies in this course tested that, and the method is not a treatment or a prevention for any illness. Dresler's trainees were young men learning word lists. Maguire's team wrote that the value of mnemonics after brain injury and in disease is less clear,1 and the 2021 meta-analysis noted that the method has had relatively few educational and clinical uses.2 If your memory worries you, talk to a doctor.
Myth Any hard memory workout will do the same job.
Reality Not in Dresler's study. Six weeks of the n-back, a demanding working-memory game, did not lift word-list recall the way loci training did: the loci group improved significantly more than both control groups, and the two control groups did not differ.3 The benefit came from the method, not from effort in general.

Wait, really? Training made brains do less, not more. In a 2021 follow-up of the same training study, Wagner and colleagues found that activity during learning and recognition fell in the lateral prefrontal, parahippocampal and retrosplenial cortex, in memory athletes and trained novices alike,4 partly linked to better memory four months on. The authors read it as a sign of neural efficiency:5 a skilled brain gets the job done with less effort, the way a practiced hand writes without thinking about each letter.
